item.title: Gazipur garment fire: Blaze brought under control after 3.5 hours
item.description:
A fire at a garment in the Degerchala Faqir Market area of Gazipur city was brought under control after around 3.5 hours of efforts at around 6pm on Saturday.
However, 70 workers fell ill from smoke after being trapped inside the factory. They were rescued by Fire Service personnel and later taken to different hospitals.
The fire broke out at around 2:45pm at the Metrix sweater factory in the Faqir Market area.
Md Saidul Alam Chowdhury, deputy assistant director of Gazipur Fire Service, said the fire started on the third floor of the factory and quickly spread to the surrounding areas.
Initially, 3 units from Gazipur Chowrasta Modern Fire Station, 1 unit from Konabari Fire Station, 2 units from Gazipur Fire Station and 2 units from Rajendrapur Fire Station joined the firefighting operation. Another unit later joined, bringing the total to 9 units.
Md Saidul Alam Chowdhury said: “The Metrix sweater factory is located in the Degerchala Faqir Market area of the city. We received information about the fire at around 2:45pm. We then began efforts to bring it under control. The fire broke out on the third floor of the building. Meanwhile, 70 people fell ill from smoke after being trapped inside. They were rescued alive and sent to different local hospitals.”
He said: “There were no ponds or other sources of water nearby, and the factory did not have its own firefighting system, which made it difficult to bring the fire under control. The cause of the fire and the extent of the damage were not immediately known. Details will be known after an investigation.”
According to another account, the fire broke out at the Metti garment factory in the Faqir Market area at around 2:45pm on Saturday.
Md Saleh Uddin, deputy director of Fire Service and Civil Defence, said: “We received information that a fire had broken out in the warehouse of the Metti garment factory. After receiving the information, 2 units from Bhogra Bypass Fire Service arrived at the scene. After seeing the intensity, size and nature of the fire, our officer on duty requested assistance. Subsequently, a total of 9 units arrived here in phases.”
He said: “Many people were trapped on the roof of the building. We brought the vehicle we use for rescue operations from high-rise buildings here. We rescued a total of 69 people from inside and from the roof of the building.”
He said: “The 3-storey building is covered with glass on all sides and it is a warehouse, making firefighting extremely risky. Our firefighters worked at risk and did so today as well. They entered the building despite the risk and applied special Fire Service techniques while enduring intense heat to bring the fire under control after 3.5 hours.”
He added: “Bringing a fire under control does not mean the fire has been extinguished. Our firefighters are still working inside. It will take some time to extinguish the fire completely. Since there was a fabric warehouse here, a lot of fabric needs to be removed. The fire has to be completely extinguished by removing the materials one by one.”
“We are also making further inquiries to find out whether there are any casualties. How the fire started and whether there were any faults in the factory will be known after the fire is extinguished and a detailed investigation is conducted.”

item.title: Shama Obaed: Bangladesh wants independent foreign policy, open to global cooperation
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Saturday said Bangladesh wants to pursue its foreign policy independently while remaining open to cooperation with the international community.
“We don't want to be a chessboard for other players to play. We want to play on our own terms. We are ready to negotiate, collaborate and partner with the rest of the world with our head held high,” she said.
Speaking at a panel discussion titled “A World Rewritten: Power, Technology and Trust in the Age of Uncertainty” as part of the 3-day Bay of Bengal Conversation, the state minister said Bangladesh is now in a position where it is holding its head high.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman spoke as the chief guest at the inaugural session.
Former President of the Republic of Serbia Boris Tadić, Distinguished Professor at Illinois State University, USA, Ali Riaz, Deputy Head of Mission at the Royal Norwegian Embassy in Bangladesh Alexander Falck-Bilden, Member of Parliament of Montenegro Gordan Stojović, and Editor-at-Large of TIME Magazine, Singapore, Charles Thomas Campbell took part in the first panel discussion.
“But of course, remembering that the most important thing in our foreign policy is the interest of our people,” Shama said.
Seeking broader international cooperation to resolve the Rohingya crisis, she said Bangladesh wants to cooperate with countries across South Asia, Asia and beyond as part of its economic diplomacy.
“As far as economic diplomacy goes, we believe in collaborating and working with all the nations in South Asia, Asia, and elsewhere. We want to collaborate with everyone. We want Bangladesh to become a hub because we have the demographic dividend,” she said.
“We have the people, and when we talk about power, I believe our people is our power,” Shama said.
The state minister said Bangladesh is seeking broader international cooperation to resolve the Rohingya crisis, stressing that the country cannot sustain the burden of hosting the refugees indefinitely.
“We don't know the exact number anymore, because it's 1.3 million plus Rohingya refugees, and the number is increasing every day because 30,000 children are being born every year, more or less. And every day there is influx going on,” she said.
Shama said Bangladesh is facing the challenge of a growing young Rohingya population in Cox's Bazar, with inadequate access to education, healthcare, food and security.
She also highlighted the security challenges Bangladesh faces due to the situation in Myanmar and developments along the border.
Shama described the situation inside Myanmar as complicated, saying that resolving the crisis requires engagement with multiple stakeholders - Arakan Army, Myanmar government, and the other entities.
She said Bangladesh is pursuing discussions with its neighbours and other countries to find a solution to the crisis.
Speaking about Bangladesh's broader foreign policy and economic priorities, Shama said Bangladesh, with a population of around 170 million, has significant potential as a trade, energy and investment hub between South and Southeast Asia.
“Basically, you know, Bangladesh is a nation of 170,000,000 people, and we see it where South Asia meets Southeast Asia on the shores of the Bay of Bengal, with unlimited potential of trade, energy, and investment,” she said.
Shama said Bangladesh faced challenges following the war situation in the Gulf, particularly in terms of energy security and the large Bangladeshi diaspora living and working in Gulf countries.
“So it reminds me that during that time, we have lost 14 of Bangladeshis who have been working in different countries in the Gulf,” she said.
Shama said the government is focusing on economic diplomacy and diversification of energy sources.
Responding to a question on artificial intelligence, Shama said Bangladesh wants technology to contribute to peace, security and stability rather than conflict.
“We want to live in a world where AI stops wars, not initiates. We want to live in a world where technology actually facilitates peace and security and stability, but does not start wars,” she said.
The state minister also said Bangladesh wants to use AI in ways that benefit different sections of society.
“We are living in the age of technology and AI, but we want to use AI in the social context of Bangladesh, where our farmers, our women entrepreneurs, our businessmen, our agriculture, our every sector of our population gets advantage of artificial intelligence, which is possible,” she said. “So that is what we are striving for,” she added.
On artificial intelligence and technology, Shama said the government is pursuing an economy based on technology and innovation, with emphasis on startups and new technologies.
“Regarding AI and technology, Bangladesh government at the present is thriving for an economy that is technology based, innovation based, and even in the new budget, in this fiscal year, our government clearly gave enough emphasis on startups and new technology and artificial intelligence-based economy,” she said.
The state minister said Bangladesh also needs to remain aware of the vulnerabilities associated with the growing use of artificial intelligence and digital technologies.
“As we embrace artificial intelligence, as we increase training in AI in Bangladesh's social context, we have to be also aware of the vulnerabilities that it creates across the board….in the cyber world, in digital world,” she said.
Shama said AI and technology are also contributing to misinformation, disinformation and digital harassment.
“Because of AI, we have misinformation, disinformation. We are seeing digital harassment against women and children, and that is created by the technology,” she said.
She called for global cooperation to address such challenges.
“It has now become a global issue. As we embrace technology, as we embrace innovation, to strengthen our economy, we also come forward and try to unite the world to combat, how we can actually address the issue of digital harassment in the cybersecurity because it's not a country-specific problem,” Shama said.

item.title: NBR raids 4 establishments, including Muqtadir’s father-in-law’s
item.description:
The National Board of Revenue (NBR) conducted coordinated raids at four establishments in Dhaka on Saturday, including a business owned by content creator Salman Muqtadir’s father-in-law, over alleged violations involving alcohol products, customs duty, value-added tax (VAT) and income tax.
Fu-Wang Bowling and Services Limited, owned by Sheikh Nur Islam, was among the establishments raided. The NBR said the operation also covered allegations of illegal sourcing of alcohol products, tax evasion and the supply of alcoholic products to unauthorized customers.
According to NBR sources, confidential information was received alleging that several bars, restaurants, diplomatic bonded warehouses and duty-free shops in Dhaka were procuring alcohol and alcohol products from illegal sources.
There were also allegations of evasion of applicable customs duty, VAT and income tax on the products and supplying them to unauthorized customers.
Following the allegations, a special operation was launched with the coordination of various agencies under the NBR.
The Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID) formed 4 separate teams for the operation. Officials from the NBR’s Income Tax Intelligence and Investigation Unit, Central Intelligence Cell (CIC), VAT Audit, Intelligence and Investigation Directorate, and Customs, Excise and VAT Commissionerate, Dhaka (North), joined the operation on Saturday.
As part of the operation, the teams conducted on-site inspections, searches and document checks at the 4 establishments. In some cases, activities to seize the relevant products were also carried out.
The establishments raided on Saturday are Raw Canvas Restaurant & Bar, Habib Hotel International Ltd, Margarita Lounge and Fu-Wang Bowling and Services Limited.
NBR sources said the quantity of alcohol and alcohol products stored at the establishments was being verified. The authorities were also checking the legal sources of the stored products, import or purchase documents, whether applicable customs duty, VAT and other taxes had been paid, and the legality of the products.
They were also investigating how the establishments procured the products and whether they were supplied through legally authorized sources and to authorized customers.
NBR officials said further legal action would be taken based on the preliminary information obtained during the operation. If any irregularities or tax evasion are found, action may be taken under the relevant laws.
The NBR has arranged a press conference on Saturday night to disclose the preliminary findings and overall results of the operation. The press conference will be held at 10:30pm on the ground floor of the National Board of Revenue in Agargaon, Dhaka.
Earlier, on Thursday, 4 warehouses belonging to Salman Muqtadir’s father-in-law Sheikh Nur Islam were sealed over allegations of storing duty-free alcohol.

item.title: Dinesh Trivedi stresses dialogue, trust to address Dhaka-Delhi issues
item.description:
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi on Saturday highlighted the need for continuous dialogue, mutual respect and trust between the two countries to address bilateral issues, saying every issue between the two neighbors has a solution.
“There’s no point hiding the issues, and there’s no point not talking about the issues,” he said while speaking at a discussion titled “Power and Prudence: Managing Great-Power Competition without Conflict” as part of the ongoing Bay of Bengal Conversation in Dhaka.
Trivedi, who faced a couple of questions, said the two countries need to discuss all outstanding issues, including water, trade, culture, sports, communication and transportation, through appropriate forums.
“In a democracy, the dialogue has to be there at the proper forum. And the dialogue has to be a continuous dialogue,” he said, noting that the process of engagement between the two countries may be slow, but it has not stopped.
“I can guarantee you, there is no stoppage of process. The process is ongoing,” Trivedi said. “Believe me, there has to be a solution, and there will be a solution,” the Indian diplomat added.
The High Commissioner said Bangladesh as an independent and sovereign country, understands its own security interests and has the right to make its own decisions.
“Bangladesh is an absolutely independent country and people have elected democratically. So whatever decision Bangladesh takes is the decision of Bangladesh government,” he said, adding that “Nobody should tell Bangladesh what they should do.”
Trivedi also said India’s relationship with Bangladesh does not depend on Dhaka’s relations with other countries.
“As far as we are concerned in India, the relationship doesn’t depend on what relation Bangladesh has with other countries,” he said. He stressed that both countries have the right to protect their respective national interests.
“They are absolutely in their very much right to protect their very interest of the peoples. So are we,” Trivedi said.
Describing Bangladesh-India ties as distinct from a merely transactional relationship, he said the two countries share deep cultural and historical bonds.
“We go through not only transactional relationship; it is much beyond which is cultural. And that cultural bond is very, very foundationally solid,” he said.
Trivedi, who said he comes from India’s eastern state of West Bengal, said he understands the historical and cultural connections between the people of the two countries.
“This relationship is very difficult for the outside world to understand, which is culturally deep-rooted,” he said.
He said the two countries’ relationship has a unique cultural foundation, referring to the shared legacy of Bengali cultural icons.
“Can you imagine that one person, Rabindranath Tagore, has written the national anthem for both the countries?” the envoy said.
The High Commissioner also said good neighbors should support each other when faced with calamities or security challenges, while respecting each other’s sovereignty and domestic policies. “At the same time, no neighbor has any reason to interfere in each other’s policies,” he said.
Trivedi acknowledged that disagreements are inevitable between neighboring democracies.
“In a family, there are hiccups, and if I say that no, there are no issues. If there are no issues, there is not democracy. In democracies, you are bound to have issues,” he said.
He said such issues can only be addressed through dialogue and consultation, with trust serving as their foundation.
“Issues can only and only be settled through dialogue, through consultation. And the basis of that dialogue is trust,” he said.
“Without dialogue, it is not possible to sort out relationship from remote. And that is what we feel that is work in progress all the time,” he added.
Trivedi expressed confidence that the strong people-to-people ties between the two countries would continue to underpin bilateral relations. “I have full confidence that it’s here to stay,” he said.
The discussion was organized to examine ways of managing strategic rivalry and reducing the risk of escalation amid growing geopolitical uncertainty.
President of the Bangladesh Institute of Peace and Security Studies Maj Gen (Retd) ANM Muniruzzaman, former Army Commander of the Indian Army Arun Kumar Sahni, Professor at Georgetown University Carol Christine Fair, and foreign relations adviser to the mayor of Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality Mustafa Osman Turan also participated in the discussion.
Managing Director of Cnsltng-Bsnss-Dvlpmnt, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Faris Hadrovic moderated the session.
Turan, who also served as Turkish Ambassador to Bangladesh, said strategic autonomy does not simply mean sitting in the middle.
“It means having the ability to make your own decisions in pursuit of your strategic interests,” he said.
Muniruzzaman said they live in an “extremely contested and fragmented” world and Bangladesh is playing the role of an aspiring middle power.
Arun Kumar Sahni said stability rests on two foundations - sovereignty from a military perspective, and trust.

HRSS: Political violence in September leaves 4 dead, 527 injured
item.description:
At least four people were killed and 527 others injured in 68 incidents of political violence across Bangladesh in September, according to a report by the Human Rights Support Society (HRSS).
The human rights organisation disclosed the figures in a press release on Saturday, saying the report was based on news published in 16 national media outlets and information gathered through its own investigations.
In August, 70 incidents of political violence left seven people dead and 536 injured, according to the report.
HRSS said the September incidents were mainly linked to political disputes, attempts to establish dominance and extortion.
Of the 68 incidents, 35 stemmed from internal conflicts within the BNP, leaving 340 people injured and one dead.
Seven clashes between the BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami left 61 people injured, while six clashes between the BNP and Awami League left 42 injured and one dead.
Two clashes between Jamaat-e-Islami and the Awami League left three people injured and one dead, while three clashes between the BNP and the National Citizens Party (NCP) injured 16 people.
Seven clashes between the BNP and other political parties left 15 people injured. Another seven clashes involving different political parties left 50 people injured and one dead.
Of the four people killed in political violence during the month, two were affiliated with the Awami League, while one each belonged to the BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami, HRSS said.
Meanwhile, at least 20 people were injured in two clashes linked to the upcoming local government elections.
The report also documented 12 separate attacks by miscreants on political leaders and activists in September. The attacks left seven people injured, including five BNP activists and one Jamaat-e-Islami activist.

item.title: CUET Students protest new VC’s remarks, seek PM’s intervention
item.description:
Students of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) staged a procession on Saturday in protest against remarks made by newly appointed Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr Sheikh Shariful Alam, which they described as “misleading and propagandistic.”
They brought out the procession around 2:30pm on the 12th day of their movement demanding the reinstatement of former Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem.
They also called for Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s intervention to resolve the ongoing deadlock at the university and restore normal academic activities.
In an interview with the media on Friday, Prof Sheikh Shariful said four examinations of the 2023-24 academic year had been stalled due to the movement.
The protesters, however, disputed the claim, saying it did not reflect the actual situation on campus. They said examinations in almost all departments of the academic year had already been completed, with only one department yet to begin its exams.
The procession began at the Shaheed Minar, passed through Swadhinata Chattar and ended at the Shaheed Minar.
During the march, students chanted slogans including, “Your VC, my VC—Sayem Sir, Sayem Sir” and “One point, one demand—We want Sayem Sir as VC.”
They carried a banner calling for the prime minister’s intervention to end the deadlock at CUET. Placards read, “Prime Minister’s intervention to restore CUET,” “CUET Revolts for Sayem Sir” and “PM, Consider Our Appeal.”
The students called for Prof Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem’s reinstatement as vice-chancellor, an end to the university’s ongoing deadlock and the restoration of a normal academic environment.
Shahriar Hisham, a third-year student of CUET’s Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering (ETE) Department, said, “We have been protesting to demand the reinstatement of Sayem Sir as vice-chancellor. We are frustrated by the administration’s silence. Classes and examinations have remained suspended because of the movement. We are seeking the prime minister’s intervention and want him to take prompt steps to resolve the crisis. We want to return to our classes.”
Students have been observing a “complete shutdown” at CUET since September 22, demanding Prof Sayem’s reinstatement. They have carried out various programmes, including red-card demonstrations and torch processions.
Regular academic activities remain suspended, while examinations of different years in six departments are currently stalled. The students have vowed to continue their movement until their demand is met.

PM Tarique shares photo with Trump from New York dinner
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday shared a photo of himself and his wife Dr Zubaida Rahman with US President Donald Trump from a dinner hosted by the US president for world leaders attending the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
The prime minister shared the photo on his Facebook page after the White House released it, showing him and Dr Zubaida Rahman with President Trump.
Trump and First Lady Melania Trump hosted the dinner on September 22 night at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel in New York for heads of state and government of UN member states and their spouses.
The dinner was held in honor of world leaders who had gathered in New York to attend the 81st session of the UNGA.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Dr Zubaida Rahman attended the dinner along with other world leaders and their spouses.
Earlier, the Prime Minister and his wife attended a breakfast hosted by UN Secretary-General António Guterres for heads of state and government and their spouses.
The White House also shared another photo featuring Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s wife Dr Zubaida Rahman and US First Lady Melania Trump during a special meeting of first ladies in New York.
The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, bringing together spouses of heads of state and government from different countries.
During the meeting, Melania Trump unveiled her global children’s welfare initiative, “Fostering the Future Together”, and called on first ladies from other countries to join the initiative.
The Prime Minister went to New York on September 21 – leading a 35-member delegation – to attend the UNGA and delivered his maiden address as Prime Minister at the General Debate on September 24.
He returned home on September 27 morning after wrapping up his five-day visit to the United States.

item.title: Ten crude bombs recovered outside Chhatra League leader’s home in Tongi
item.description:
Police recovered 10 crude bombs from a sack placed in front of the home of outlawed Chhatra League leader Nur Nabi Hossain, alias Hridoy, 22, in Tongi, Gazipur, along with 2 banners of the outlawed Awami League beside the sack on Saturday, October 3.
Hridoy is the organizational secretary of Tongi West thana Chhatra League.
The crude bombs were recovered from Tongi’s Gutiya Andarul area early Saturday and later neutralized by the police bomb disposal unit in the afternoon.
Police and locals said residents saw the crude bombs lying in front of Hridoy’s home in the morning and informed police. A team from Tongi West police station later went to the spot, recovered the crude bombs and cordoned off the surrounding area for security.
Tongi West police station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Arifur Rahman confirmed the recovery of 10 crude bombs and 2 banners.
He said the 2 recovered banners announced a protest procession demanding the cancellation of the ban on the Awami League, cancellation of the court verdict and release of imprisoned individuals.
The banners carried the names of several leaders and activists of Tongi West thana and Ward 52 Jubo League and Chhatra League. One banner named Farid, Habibur Rahman, Babul and Ali Akbar as aspirants for various posts in Ward 52 Jubo League.
The other banner named Tongi West thana Chhatra League organizational secretary Nur Nabi Hossain, alias Hridoy, Sajid Hossain Dipu, and Ward 52 Chhatra League’s Hasan Nahid and Sajib.
It could not immediately be confirmed who had placed the crude bombs there or whether there was any connection between the explosives and the banners.
An investigation is underway to identify those involved, while the crude bombs have been neutralized. Legal action will be taken against those involved based on the investigation, police said.
Mohammad Arifur Rahman said: “We suspect that miscreants left the crude bombs there with the intention of sabotage. After they were recovered, the police bomb disposal unit was informed. Members of the unit came from Dhaka and safely neutralized the crude bombs at around 4pm.”

item.title: Dengue: Six more die, 1,608 hospitalized in 24 hours
item.description:

The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) confirmed the figures in a press release on Saturday. According to DGHS data, the dengue death toll has risen to 256 this year, with 148 deaths recorded in September alone.
So far this year, 84,369 people have been hospitalized with dengue across the country.

DMP commissioner: Gulistan, Fulbaria bus terminals to shift within 3 months
item.description:
Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Commissioner Mosleh Uddin Ahmed has said the Gulistan and Fulbaria bus terminals in the capital will be relocated to Chunkutia in Keraniganj within 3 months.
He made the remarks while speaking to journalists after inspecting traffic management development activities at the Mohakhali terminal on Saturday.
The DMP commissioner said 10 acres of land would be provided at the Jhilmil project in Chunkutia for use as a depot.
“Jhilmil has already given us permission, and we have started work on the depot there,” he said.
The DMP commissioner said around 75 more acres of land would be available there through the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (Rajuk).
A permanent terminal and depot will be established on the land. There are plans to relocate all transport vehicles and trucks serving 19 districts in the southern region, along with trucks from the Badamtali wholesale market.
Asked how long the process would take, he said: “We have set a maximum timeframe of 3 months. We hope the work will be completed within these 3 months. As soon as the work is completed, the buses from Fulbaria and Gulistan will be shifted there.”
Regarding traffic management at the Mohakhali terminal, the DMP commissioner said: “This will operate under a disciplined system. If anyone attempts even minor irregularities, we will take strict legal action.”
At the event, Member of Parliament Md Shamsur Rahman Simul Biswas said: “We are all frustrated with the intolerable traffic congestion in Dhaka city and the disorder in the road transport sector. We want to change this situation.”

Bank Asia, BB sign participation agreements for green industries, ICT financing
item.description:
Bank Asia PLC has signed two participation agreements with Bangladesh Bank, becoming a participating financial institution (PFI) under the central bank’s refinance schemes for green factory buildings and industries and ICT sector development.
AKM Nurunnabi, director of the Sustainable Finance Department of Bangladesh Bank, and Sohail RK Hussain, managing director of Bank Asia, signed the agreements at a ceremony recently held at the Bangladesh Bank Head Office in Dhaka.
Under the Tk2,000 crore schemes, Bangladesh Bank provides access to low-cost financing to support the development of green factory buildings and industries, as well as projects in the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) sector.
As a participating financial institution, Bank Asia will facilitate refinance-supported financing for eligible entrepreneurs investing in sustainable industrial development and ICT-related initiatives.
The participation reinforces Bank Asia’s commitment to sustainable finance, responsible banking and inclusive economic growth.

item.title: BB expands export pre-shipment refinance fund to Tk7,000cr
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has expanded its pre-shipment credit refinance facility for export-oriented industries from Tk5,000 crore to Tk7,000 crore, while raising the maximum customer-level interest rate on new loans from 5% to 6%.
The central bank announced the decision in a circular issued by its Banking Regulation and Policy Department-1 on Thursday, stating that the measure aims to sustain export operations and bolster foreign exchange earnings amid economic realities.
To facilitate the expansion, the central bank reallocated Tk2,000 crore from its Tk10,000-crore Export Facilitation Pre-finance Fund (EFPF) into the pre-shipment scheme, bringing the remaining balance of the EFPF down to Tk3,000 crore.
Under the revised structure, participating commercial banks can charge end borrowers a maximum interest rate of 6% per annum.
Correspondingly, the refinancing rate charged by Bangladesh Bank to participating institutions has been raised to 3% from the previous 2%, maintaining a 3% margin for the intermediary banks.

Dhaka Tribune journalist Shahrukh selected for COP31 fellowship
item.description:
Dhaka Tribune journalist Shaikh Shahrukh Farhan has been selected for the 2026 Climate Change Media Partnership (CCMP) Reporting Fellowship to cover the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20.
Shahrukh is among 14 journalists and two independent creator-journalists selected from Asia, Africa, Europe, Latin America and the Pacific through an international selection process.
The fellowship is jointly organized by the Earth Journalism Network (EJN), Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.
Under the program, the selected journalists will report directly from the UN climate negotiations, covering international climate policy and its implications for audiences in their respective countries.
For Bangladesh, Shahrukh’s reporting is expected to focus on the implications of COP31 negotiations for a country facing climate-related challenges, including rising temperatures, extreme weather, sea-level rise and coastal erosion.
The fellowship will enable participants to cover negotiations and developments involving climate finance, infrastructure, greenhouse gas emissions reduction, mitigation and adaptation.
Participants will also receive professional guidance from journalists and media trainers Joydeep Gupta, Fermín Koop and Imelda Abaño.
The program brings together journalists from 15 countries, providing opportunities to exchange reporting experiences and strengthen their understanding of international climate negotiations.
Other selected fellows include Anandabhuwana from Indonesia, Angelica Maria Daza Romero from Colombia, Aparna Bose from India, Aria Deemie from Liberia, Hammad S from Pakistan, Lerato Mutsila from South Africa, María de los Ángeles Graterol Camacho from Venezuela, Maria Vasileva Petrova-Galabova from Bulgaria, Nadia Luna from Argentina, Nathalie Iriarte Villavicencio from Bolivia, Nkoli Omhoudu from Nigeria, Noel Charles Piringi from Solomon Islands, Francis Ontomwa from Kenya and Zenebe Hailu Gemechu from Ethiopia.
Shahrukh has more than 12 years of experience in journalism, covering public policy, governance, climate change, environmental protection, energy, ICT and telecommunications, elections, migration, women and children, and sustainable development.
His reporting interests include climate adaptation, renewable energy, energy security, environmental pollution, biodiversity conservation, climate finance and issues affecting climate-vulnerable communities.
COP31, the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, is scheduled to take place in Antalya from November 9 to 20.
The conference will bring together government representatives, international organizations, researchers, civil society groups and other stakeholders for negotiations on global climate action.
Key issues expected to feature in reporting from the conference include countries’ climate commitments, progress on previous agreements, climate finance, mitigation and adaptation.

item.title: Dinajpur entrepreneur cultivates black rice for first time in Bochaganj
item.description:
A young entrepreneur has experimentally cultivated Vietnamese black rice for the first time in Bochaganj upazila of Dinajpur, drawing interest from local farmers over its potential profitability.
Rakibul Haque, a resident of Dighori village in Nafanagar Union who cultivated the crop on 33 decimals of leased land, said he became interested in black rice after learning about it online. He first bought 1kg of rice for Tk550 to taste it before deciding to cultivate the crop. He later purchased 2kg of seeds online for Tk1,150 and raised seedlings.
Unable to secure permission to use his family’s ancestral land, he leased 33 decimals for Tk24,000 and transplanted the seedlings on July 9. The crop is expected to be harvested between October 10 and 12. “Black rice does not require additional fertiliser, irrigation or special care compared with conventional rice,” Rakibul said.
He expects to harvest 18-20 maunds of rice from the plot. With black rice currently selling for around Tk400 per kg, he expects potential sales of about Tk320,000 if the projected yield and market price are achieved.
According to the agriculture department, black rice is rich in antioxidants, anthocyanin, fibre and iron. Its nutritional value has made it popular among health-conscious consumers, while it is also sought after by Chinese restaurants.
Local residents have been visiting the field ahead of the harvest, and some have contacted Rakibul to collect seeds for future cultivation. Local farmers Shambhu Roy and Jewel said they were interested in growing black rice after seeing the crop’s growth and condition.
Rakibul’s father, Aminul Haque, initially opposed the project, calling his son’s internet-inspired venture “madness” and refusing to provide ancestral land. He has since changed his mind after seeing the crop’s progress. “I am ready to support my son in any way I can after seeing the success of his initiative,” he said.
Bochaganj Upazila Agriculture Officer Nayan Kumar Saha said wider cultivation of the nutrient-rich rice could contribute to the country’s agricultural economy.
Upazila Nirbahi Officer Md Maruf Hasan said this was the first black rice cultivation in Bochaganj. “If production and marketing can be properly ensured, it could be a profitable crop for farmers,” he said.

item.title: Fruit prices soar in Bandarban
item.description:
Prices of various fruits have surged in Bandarban, with traders attributing the rise in prices of oranges, maltas and pomegranates to increased demand amid a dengue outbreak.
Prices of oranges and maltas have increased by up to Tk200 per kilogram in the past two weeks, putting fruits beyond the reach of many patients and middle-income families.
A visit to Bandarban’s fruit market on Friday found that the price of malta had risen from Tk270 to Tk450 per kg, while Chinese oranges increased from Tk280 to Tk500. Pomegranates rose from Tk380 to Tk460 per kg.
Gala apples increased from Tk340 to Tk360, Fuji Gala apples from Tk320 to Tk330, pears from Tk300 to Tk310 and red grapes from Tk400 to Tk440 per kg.
White grapes, which were previously unavailable in the market, are now selling for Tk500 per kg. Watermelon prices have also risen from Tk80 to Tk90 per kg.
Mohammad Abdul Alim of Siddiq Store, a fruit trader at Bandarban market, said demand had not increased significantly. “Fruit prices are high because our purchase costs have increased. So, we have to sell them at higher prices,” he said.
Papayas, commonly included in the diets of dengue patients, are also in short supply. Meanwhile, large coconuts have risen from Tk120 to Tk160 each, while small ones now sell for Tk120, up from Tk110.
Champak Das, a coconut trader, said demand for coconuts had increased amid the dengue outbreak while supplies had fallen. “When supply falls against higher demand, prices go up. We have little scope to sell them at lower prices,” he said.
According to the Bandarban civil surgeon’s office, 1,095 people have contracted dengue in the district between January 1 and October 2. Two people have died, both from Rowangchhari upazila.
Akim Bom, who was buying fruit for a patient, said the price hikes were making it increasingly difficult for families to afford fruit. “If prices keep rising like this, we may not be able to continue buying fruit,” he said.
Traders expect prices of imported fruits to ease somewhat toward the end of October as the winter season begins and supplies increase.

item.title: ‘Shanti Nibas’ remains closed for three years in Rajshahi, Khulna
item.description:
A ‘Shanti Nibas’ (old home), built by the government for abandoned and destitute elderly people in Rajshahi at a cost of nearly Tk 9 crore, has remained closed for three years. The Shanti Nibas in Baya area of Paba upazila was inaugurated three years ago with facilities to accommodate 25 elderly people, including healthcare, lift, recreation, exercise, prayer, and training facilities.
But not a single elderly person has been admitted to the facility due to a lack of manpower recruitment. Besides, an organogram for its operation has yet to be prepared.
The facility was built under a government program to provide safe accommodation and care for people aged over 60 who are abandoned, destitute, or have no one to look after them. In 2020, Department of Social Services took up a project to build 25-bed Shanti Nibas facilities on the premises of government children’s homes in eight divisions.
In Rajshahi, a three-storey building with a five-storey foundation was constructed on 1,621 square metres of land on the western side of Paba Government Children’s Home (Boys). It has 25 beds, a lift, reception and visitors’ rooms, a healthcare corner, recreation and exercise equipment, a prayer room, a training corner, a production unit, and a coffee corner.
Despite the infrastructure being ready, the facility has remained closed to its intended beneficiaries. Long periods of disuse have left dust on furniture and equipment, while moss has formed on parts of the walls. Some equipment is also at risk of deterioration.
Rajshahi Social Services Department Deputy Director Monira Khatun said the facility could not be opened because the necessary manpower had not been appointed. “An organogram for recruiting the required manpower has not even been prepared. So far, we have not been able to admit any elderly person,” she said.
Besides, a Shanti Nibas built in Khulna to provide shelter for abandoned and destitute elderly people has remained closed for nearly three years due to a lack of staff appointments and an official office code.
The facility, built inside the government children’s family premises in Maheshwarpasha, was formally inaugurated on November 14, 2023. However, it has yet to accommodate a single resident. The three-storey building, constructed on a five-storey foundation, can house 25 elderly people.
A recent visit found moss on the stairs, balconies and walls, while railings have started rusting. Furniture and equipment have also been gathering dust. Some fire extinguishers at the facility have expired.
The ground floor has a doctors’ room equipped with a bed, wheelchairs and a therapy bed, while exercise equipment remains unused in the gym. The dining room has two large tables.
“The furniture and other equipment are deteriorating to some extent as the facility has remained unused for so long,” said Khan Motahar Hossain, deputy director of the divisional social services office. “It could not be opened due to the absence of staff appointments and an office code,” he added.

Democracy cannot survive with a fearful press
item.description:
That at least 162 journalists across the country faced attacks, threats, and legal harassment in 112 separate incidents over the past three months while performing their professional duties, according to a monitoring report by private research organization Media Initiative for Development (MID), should alarm us.
When members of the media are systematically targeted simply for documenting public events, investigating corruption, or asking uncomfortable questions, it signals a dangerous erosion of basic rights.
A nation striving to rebuild its democratic institutions cannot succeed while those tasked with holding power accountable operate under constant fear for their safety.
In any functioning democracy, an independent press serves as the eyes and ears of the public, tasked with providing citizens with the objective facts necessary to make informed decisions.
When media workers are assaulted by political cadres, intimidated by influential interest groups, or subjected to arbitrary legal harassment, it is not merely an attack on individual reporters but a direct assault on the public's right to know.
This hostility toward journalism reflects a deep-seated, systemic culture of intolerance that has unfortunately persisted across political transitions, and has only been exacerbated as a result of the technology-enabled society we live in today.
When law enforcement agencies fail to protect working journalists on the ground or, worse, turn a blind eye to political mobs targeting newsrooms, it creates a chilling effect that fosters self-censorship.
It goes without saying that a media environment gripped by fear cannot fulfill its democratic mandate. Protecting press freedom requires more than public declarations but rather demands physical security, legal safeguards, and an environment where journalists can report without fear of retribution.
Democracy cannot survive without truth, and truth cannot surface when the press is silenced.

item.title: Revenue generation needs long-term planning
item.description:
The International Monetary Fund’s critical assessment of the National Board of Revenue’s (NBR) latest reform roadmap exposes a fundamental truth that has been an issue for Bangladesh for years: Short term, superficial administrative adjustments cannot resolve our chronic fiscal woes.
Despite repeated pledges to modernize tax collection and broaden the revenue base, it is disappointing that the NBR remains crippled by structural loopholes, slow execution, and a reliance on ad-hoc targets.
For a country maintaining one of the lowest tax-to-GDP ratios in South Asia , hovering under 8%, we must stop treating tax reform as a bureaucratic compliance exercise rather than the national priority it is.
The IMF’s critique rightly targets the core flaws of our revenue architecture. Rather than pursuing systemic modernization through comprehensive digitization, structural decoupling of tax policy from enforcement, and the elimination of discretionary exemptions, the revenue authority routinely defaults to squeezing existing taxpayers.
Setting ambitious revenue targets without fixing systemic leakages or curbing widespread tax evasion yields predictable shortfalls year after year. Furthermore, the persistent delay in fully automating tax administration and streamlining VAT collection perpetuates an environment ripe for rent-seeking and corruption.
Bangladesh can no longer afford an inefficient revenue apparatus. With growing debt-servicing obligations, rising social spending needs, and critical infrastructure demands, sustainable fiscal health depends on a modern, equitable, and transparent tax system.
As such, we hope and expect those at NBR to recognize that we learn to plan for the long term. For that to happen, we must start focusing on high-income earners and corporate entities currently operating outside official channels, rather than overburdening compliant businesses and middle-class citizens through indirect taxation.
Real reform requires genuine political will, not administrative posturing to satisfy multilateral lenders. Until the government replaces half-hearted measures with deep, structural reform, our fiscal stability will remain shaky.

Russia warns diplomats to leave Kyiv over new strikes threat
item.description:
Russia on Saturday issued a new call for diplomats and foreigners to leave Kyiv, warning the Ukrainian capital of new “massive” air attacks hours after striking another major bridge in the city.
Moscow has ramped up its pummeling of Kyiv, launching waves of drones at the city, targeting key infrastructure and putting the capital on a near-constant state of alert against attacks.
The strike on the Northern Bridge on Saturday morning wounded two people and damaged road surface and trolleybus overhead wires restricting traffic, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
AFP reporters saw traces of an explosion on a pedestrian walkway and technicians repairing power lines on the bridge.
Hours after the attack, the Russian authorities warned of more strikes, issuing a fresh call for diplomats and foreigners to leave the city and refrain from visiting Ukraine.
“We note with concern that not everyone has heeded these warnings, and that individuals are knowingly exposing themselves to mortal danger,” the Russian foreign ministry said in a statement.
The Russian ministry also stated that “responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning.”
Moscow issued a similar warning in May but heads of state and governments from countries backing Ukraine have defied it by travelling to the war-torn country and the capital in show of support.
On Friday, Klitschko said the city was in a “very dramatic situation” and should now be on a war footing as the enemy was “tearing Kyiv apart” with strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure.
President Volodymyr Zelensky accused his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, of ripping up the rulebook of armed conflict by sanctioning massive attacks on civilian areas, an accusation the Kremlin has rejected.
Kyiv has been increasingly under aerial bombardment in recent months, with the attacks and alerts disrupting daily life and sowing traffic chaos.
Long lines of stationary cars and buses clogged major roads on Friday as commuters sought alternate routes, with some forced to continue their journeys on foot.
Air raid sirens warning of approaching threats sound almost round the clock, urging the city’s estimated three million people to seek shelter.
Strikes across the country in recent days have also caused power outages in several regions in the east, north and center, with grid operator Ukrenergo urging consumers to limit usage even as demand increases with colder weather.
Ukraine braces for another difficult winter. Last year, heating and power were cut for days on end as temperatures plunged to -20°C.
The grinding war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, has turned into Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.
Ukraine has appeared to stabilize the front in recent months, but depleted air-defense stocks since the start of the US-Israeli war in Iran have left its cities exposed to Russian barrages.
The US-brokered peace efforts are effectively frozen as Moscow has shown no signs of dropping its maximalist conditions to end the war, including a demand that Ukraine cede territory in the east that Russia’s troops have not captured.

item.title: Loud explosions heard in Yemen capital
item.description:
Loud explosions were heard in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa on Saturday, as the Houthis reported airstrikes in the area by Saudi forces.
One correspondent heard at least five blasts in different areas, while another saw two warplanes firing missiles on the city.
Al-Masirah TV, a Houthi-affiliated media outlet, reported “Saudi aggression” against the capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties.
The channel had also earlier on Saturday reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in the northwestern governorate of Saada, a Houthi stronghold.
Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July, the Houthis claimed.
After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is backed by neighboring Saudi Arabia.
The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country’s south and east -- a region that is larger but less populated.
Hostilities were reignited after fours years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation.
The flight did not seek authorization from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade.
Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022.
Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive which saw them seize control of coastal regions along the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.
They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
Fighting in recent days has centered on Taiz, where 80 combatants in the conflict were reported dead on Friday by sources on both sides.
The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died.
The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to wrest control of Taiz city, which is Yemen’s third-largest after Sanaa and Aden.
The Houthis also on Friday that Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours.
Saudi authorities meanwhile reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border.
Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.
On Saturday US media outlet Axios reported that top cabinet members in the Trump administration met the day before to discuss Yemen as well as the Iran conflict, citing three US officials.
The meeting was not officially announced.

item.title: 20 die in Nigerian road accident
item.description:
A multiple-vehicle road crash on a highway has killed 20 people in north-central Nigeria’s Plateau State, authorities said in a statement.
The accident on Friday afternoon on the Hawan Kibo-Jos road involved four vehicles -- a truck, car, bus and motorcycle, Nigeria’s Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) said.
“Preliminary findings indicate brake failure and subsequent loss of control as the likely causes of the crash,” FRSC spokesman Osondu Ohaeri said.
“The crash involved 25 people; 23 males and 2 females with five persons, comprising three males and two females, sustaining injuries, while 20 males sadly lost their lives.”
Road accidents are frequent in Nigeria, where roads are often poorly maintained and traffic rules are widely flouted.
Some 10,446 accidents caused 5,289 deaths in 2025, according to FRSC statistics.
At least 1,347 fatalities were recorded in road crashes in the first quarter of 2026, according to the Nigerian Bureau of Statistics.

item.title: Can there be solar for all, everywhere by 2030?
item.description:
In a world set ablaze by war and global warming, with ever-worsening climate disasters such as wildfires in Europe and collapsing glaciers in Nepal, solar energy provides a solution in the form of clean, affordable power, prominent climate leaders wrote in an open letter.
Signed by author Bill McKibben, former UN Climate Secretary Christiana Figueres and Canada’s former Minister of Environment and Climate Change Catherine McKenna, the letter makes a clear call. It urges governments, businesses, institutions and the public to come together to provide clean, affordable energy to “everyone, everywhere by 2030” — from the close to one billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels.
With just a little over three years to go until the decade is out, how realistic is this push?
“It’s an ambitious target, but we’ve blown away in terms of where we thought we would be on solar and renewables,” McKenna told DW. “So let’s just keep on going.”
According to global energy think tank Ember, solar power has grown at its highest rate in eight years. In 2025, it increased by a record 30% over the previous year and has risen more than tenfold since 2015.
Solar is the cheapest form of electricity in the history of the world, said McKenna, who founded the climate advisory firm Climate and Nature Solutions, and the global coalition Women Leading on Climate.
“It is scaling way faster than anyone ever imagined.”
As is battery technology used to store excess renewable energy.
“The cost of batteries have as well come down as the cost of solar modules,” said Eicke Weber, a physicist and former director of Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems who went on to found the European Solar Manufacturing Council, among other things.
“We have the technologies available and we have enough money to finance it,” he said, of a transition to widespread solar access.
In 2025, for the first time in 100 years, renewable energy sources overtook coal power in the global electricity mix, Ember’s most recent analysis showed.
At the moment, installed solar capacity around the world stands at 3 terawatts. 1TW equals 1000 gigawatts, and a single nuclear power plant has a capacity of 1GW.
Currently, the world produces about 1TW of new photovoltaic capacity each year, most of it in China. Weber says in order to fully change global energy supply to renewables, we would need about 50TW, adding that “we have more production capacities than we are selling.”
Roughly 655 million people still lack access to electricity.
“The pace of electrification in Sub-Saharan Africa has to triple to achieve universal access by 2030,” McKenna said, pointing out how quickly this gap could be closed with solar.
Areas without electricity have the opportunity to leapfrog straight into clean technologies, she says, bypassing the fossil fuels that are heating the planet. Rising global temperatures are fueling extreme weather events such as drought, storms and flooding around the world.
“And there’s a misunderstanding, which is often propagated intentionally by fossil fuel companies, that it’s expensive, it’s hard, it’s unreliable. And that just isn’t the case anymore,” she said. “To be honest, the most unreliable thing is if you’re trying to pass fossil fuels through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Hans-Josef Fell is used to the argument that certain things cannot be done. Widely known as a pioneer of renewable energy, he drafted Germany’s Renewable Energy Sources Act, which established feed-in tariffs that catalyzed clean energy growth at home and beyond.
“The Renewable Energy Sources Act unleashed exponential growth that shattered every assumption about what was achievable. It overturned the scenarios and projections that policymakers and experts had considered realistic. In the end, reality outperformed all expectations,” said Fell, who now heads the think tank Energy Watch Group.
Fell, who has lived off grid for five years, said achieving a global energy transition requires political and societal will that is “currently lacking around the world because public debate is dominated by fossil fuel interests.”
According to calculations by his think tank, if global energy demand were met entirely by renewables, solar energy would account for roughly 60-70% of the supply. The rest would come from wind power, and other sources, such as bioenergy and hydropower.
Countries like China and Pakistan have already pushed ahead.
“It is in our hands right now in the year 2026 to say we drop everything, we concentrate on this problem. We don’t need to wait for new research,” Weber said.
“It is possible to achieve this, but it would require a very kind of moonshot program,” he added, saying it would need serious political backing.
He says while it might be possible for Germany to pull off such as transition in two or three years, if the political will were there, it would likely take longer to achieve on a global scale. “We would need probably till 2040 to say that we have a goal of a worldwide 80%, 90% electricity from renewables.”
“I would sum it up this way: If we as a global society tackle this properly, we might actually be able to make it happen,” Fell said. “And even if we achieve only 90% of that goal, it would still be a remarkable accomplishment.”
McKenna pointed to the need for blended finance, calling on governments, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the private sector to put in money.
“What is irrational is continuing down the road of fossil fuels,” she added. “That’s irrational on the costs, the risks, the impacts. It’s an old technology.”

ULAB roundtable calls for reform in research and publication practices
item.description:
Academics at a national roundtable in Dhaka have called for greater responsibility and reform in research assessment, publication practices and institutional policies in Bangladesh’s humanities and social sciences.
The national roundtable on “Responsible Research and Publication in the Humanities” was organized by the Department of English and Humanities at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB) on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at the ULAB campus. Scholars and academic leaders from public and private universities took part.
Convened and moderated by Dr Abu Saleh Mohammad Rafi, Associate Professor at ULAB, the discussion examined research quality and purpose, publication choices, citation practices, authorship and mentorship, generative AI, research assessment and institutional responsibilities.
Professor Shamsad Mortuza, Vice Chancellor of ULAB, inaugurated the roundtable by discussing changes in research in literature and language. He noted that formal research training had historically received less attention in humanities disciplines such as English, while scholarly publication has grown, particularly in applied linguistics.
“Our first generation scholars did not actually focus on this trend of publication…because they were more interested in expanding knowledge in humanities,” Professor Mortuza said.
He discussed pressure on university departments to meet publication benchmarks set by “institutional masters” and “ranking markets,” noting that ranking bodies often treat arts and humanities departments as a liability because their publication metrics are generally lower than those of the sciences.
He warned against unethical practices including purchasing affiliations, publishing in predatory journals and buying citations. He also suggested interdisciplinary collaboration to increase publication output and share resources, particularly in response to what he described as systematic gatekeeping in academic publishing and distribution.
Professor Shaila Sultana of BRAC University said meaningful research should address specific problems and bring changes within communities to create real-world impact. Professor Mohammad Shafiqul Islam, PhD, of Shahjalal University of Science and Technology, said research helps develop an understanding of human existence and reinterpret existing knowledge.
Dr Nazia Manzoor of North South University said research should challenge hegemonic assumptions and generate new insights into social phenomena and policymaking.
The participants discussed publication choices and national journal indexing, noting that Bangladesh currently has no Scopus-indexed journals dedicated to the humanities or social sciences.
They also discussed the emphasis on journal articles in university promotion, while book chapters and monographs published by prestigious presses such as Oxford and Cambridge may receive less recognition. Professor Sultana said the tension between metric-driven promotion requirements and deeper qualitative inquiry remains a challenge for Bangladeshi academics.
Professor Islam said publication in leading journals of established presses is often rigorous and demanding, while the publishing industry in South Asian countries significantly lags behind global practices.
Professor Sultana and Dr Manzoor questioned why scholarly communication such as blogs and newspapers should necessarily be considered inferior to academic journals. They also questioned the emphasis on Scopus indexing and citation-based university rankings, as well as why creative writing and translation are not treated as serious scholarship in academic promotion systems.
Qumrul Hasan Chowdhury, PhD, of the University of Dhaka, said balancing national and international publication remains difficult because many scholars consider local journals inherently inferior.
He shared his experience of editing and managing national journals, saying submissions are often insufficient. He also noted that papers co-authored by senior scholars and graduate students can sometimes fall below expected standards.
Professor Anwar H Joarder, PhD, Director of the Office of Faculty Research at ULAB, said: “Citation counts are not necessarily a reliable measure of the depth or breadth of intellectual contribution.”
Professor Farzana Yesmen Chowdhury, PhD, of the University of Chittagong, said citation rates often vary by research domain and noted that limited access to open-access journals in public universities may hinder citation rates for some faculty members.
The discussion also covered article processing charges (APCs), with participants discouraging researchers from publishing in journals with high APCs. Professor Sultana said pressure on young scholars to publish rapidly can push them toward questionable paid journals.
The participants also discussed authorship ethics, particularly the balance between supporting students and maintaining academic integrity. They advocated incorporating research ethics into university curricula.
Generative AI was also discussed, with Professor Chowdhury reflecting on its implications for research practices and integrity. Speakers suggested that universities develop clear policies defining acceptable uses of AI in research and require researchers to acknowledge its use where applicable.
The discussants emphasized stronger institutional support, including adequate funding, travel grants and research facilities before research begins, rather than focusing primarily on completed research outputs.
They noted that heavy teaching loads can limit faculty members’ time for quality research and suggested that universities establish 2 tracks—one focused on teaching excellence and another on research intensity. They also emphasized that research should inform teaching practice, creating a symbiotic relationship between teaching and research.
Dr Rafi concluded the discussion, followed by closing remarks from Arifa Ghani Rahman, Head of the Department of English and Humanities at ULAB.
Rahman said: “We seem to be losing sight of the real purpose of research – not just to add new knowledge but to also solve real-world problems because of institutions’ needs to be ranked which requires publications from faculty members, often causing duress.”
She thanked the speakers and encouraged the conversation to continue.

item.title: WHO: Heart disease remains world’s biggest killer
item.description:
Ischaemic heart disease is still the world's deadliest condition; meanwhile, Covid-19 has been among the global top 10 causes of death for the first time since the pandemic began, according to the latest World Health Organization (WHO) data released on Friday.
In 2023, the top 10 causes of death made up 33 million out of 61 million deaths worldwide, which is 54% of the total.
Eight of these ten were noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), and they alone caused 47% of all deaths.
Ischaemic heart disease led to 9.5 million deaths in 2023, which is about 16% of deaths worldwide.
Since 2000, deaths from this disease have increased by 3 million, the biggest rise among all causes.
Stroke was the second leading cause, with about 6.8 million deaths (11%), followed by chronic obstructive pulmonary disease at 3.6 million (6%).
Lower respiratory infections were fourth and became the world's deadliest communicable disease again, killing 2.7 million people, which is back to pre-pandemic 2019 levels.
Alzheimer's disease and other dementias were the fifth leading cause, with 2.1 million deaths. Two-thirds of those who died were women.
Diabetes was sixth, causing 2 million deaths, which is more than twice the number in 2000.
Lung cancers were seventh, with deaths rising from 1.1 million in 2000 to 1.8 million.
Kidney diseases moved from seventeenth to ninth place, with deaths increasing by 86% since 2000.
Covid-19 was the top cause of death worldwide in 2021, with about 9.4 million deaths. By 2023, direct deaths dropped to 0.9 million, making it the fourteenth leading cause.
HIV/AIDS deaths have dropped by 62% since 2000, moving from seventh to twenty-second place.
Bangladesh is in the World Bank's lower-middle-income group, where the WHO reports a mixed disease burden.
In this group, five of the top ten causes of death were NCDs, four were communicable, maternal, neonatal, or nutritional conditions, and one was road injury.
Between 2000 and 2023, deaths from ischaemic heart disease, stroke, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease roughly doubled. These now rank in the top three.
Diabetes moved from fifteenth to fifth place, with deaths more than tripling.
Tuberculosis and diarrhoeal diseases are still in the top 10 for this group, but deaths from both have dropped by more than half over the period.
However, the WHO report does not provide country-level figures for Bangladesh.
The report shows big differences by income level.
In low-income countries, seven of the top ten causes of death were communicable diseases, with lower respiratory infections leading for most years since about 2010.
Annual deaths from the disease have exceeded 350,000 throughout 2000-2023, with no notable downward trend.
In upper-middle-income countries, lung cancer deaths more than doubled, with 520,000 more deaths.
Covid-19 is still in the top 10 only in this group.
In high-income countries, NCDs made up nine of the ten leading causes of death.
Deaths from heart disease and stroke fell by 18% and 26%, respectively, since 2000, though dementia deaths nearly quadrupled and it became the third leading cause of death.
The WHO emphasized that reliable mortality data is crucial for setting health priorities, allocating resources, and making policies in areas like transport, food, agriculture, and environmental protection.
However, it noted that data collection remains a major challenge, especially in many low-income countries where systems are often fragmented, incomplete, or inconsistent.

item.title: UK maritime agency: Oil tankers attacked in Hormuz strait
item.description:
Two oil tankers have been struck by "unidentified projectiles" in the Strait of Hormuz region, a British maritime agency said Friday, in the latest threat to shipping in the waterway.
The Hormuz passage, through which a fifth of the world's oil and LNG passed before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February and sparked the Middle East war, remains at the heart of the conflict.
Tehran has been blocking the passage of commercial ships, firing on vessels it accuses of unauthorised crossings.
Washington responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting its oil.
The first attack caused "a small fire and blackout onboard", the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said Friday, adding that the fire was later extinguished.
There were no reported casualties or environmental impact, it added.
The vessel, which was exiting the strait, was able to resume its journey, UKMTO said, without specifying the ship's ports of origin and destination.
Hours later, another crude oil tanker reported being struck by an "unknown projectile" east of Oman, with all crew safe and no environmental damage reported, according to the UKMTO.
The agency said authorities were investigating the incidents.

item.description:
A uranium consignment for the second unit of Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant reached the project site in Pabna on Saturday afternoon amid tight security.
Three uranium-laden lorries arrived at the nuclear power plant site around 12:25pm after leaving Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at around 7:15am under the security escort of the Bangladesh Army, said Pabna Deputy Commissioner Aminul Islam.
The consignment is the first shipment of uranium for the second unit of the Rooppur plant.
A special cargo aircraft carrying the uranium landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at around 11:44pm on Friday.
After completing the necessary formalities, the uranium was transported to Rooppur in three lorries while another vehicle carried other equipment.
A team of specialists who had arrived from Russia also accompanied the consignment.
Members of the Bangladesh Army, police and various intelligence agencies were deployed to ensure security during the transportation.
The flight carrying uranium for Rooppur plant was scheduled to arrive on September 24 but was not given permission to use Pakistani airspace.
According to project officials, a total of nine uranium consignments are scheduled to be brought to Bangladesh — seven for the second unit and two for the refuelling of the first unit.
All the consignments are scheduled to be delivered by December.
Fuel for the first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was brought to Bangladesh in 2023.
The Rooppur plant, comprising two 1,200-megawatt units, has a total generation capacity of 2,400MW.
Construction of the plant began in 2013 with Russian assistance at an estimated cost of more than Tk1.13 lakh crore.
Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Ltd (NPCBL) Managing Director Dr Zahidul Hasan said testing of the 16-megawatt high-pressure system under the reactor protection and safety-related system was successfully completed on Wednesday following the replacement of a defective valve.

North Korea fires ballistic missile after Seoul’s apology demand
item.description:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile, Seoul’s military said Saturday, days after demanding an apology for a blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ that it blames on the North.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility for last month’s explosion inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) and called South Korea “despicable” on Friday, undercutting overtures by Seoul’s civilian leadership seeking a return to dialogue.
Early Saturday, “our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea,” Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
“South Korea, the US, and Japan are maintaining a robust defense posture through close information sharing regarding North Korean ballistic missiles,” it said, adding the missile flew more than 700 kilometers (435 miles).
Seoul and the US-led United Nations Command found that last month’s explosion inside the DMZ, the heavily mined buffer dividing the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice, was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South side of the border.
North Korea’s military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off following leader Kim Jong Un’s designation of South Korea as his country’s “principal enemy” in 2024.
The mines responsible for the blast, which left three soldiers wounded, were believed to have been laid as part of Pyongyang’s border fortification work, according to South Korea’s defense minister Kang Shin-chul.
South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” on Friday and once again denied Pyongyang was behind the blasts.
She ridiculed Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch” and said the military’s demand her country apologize was “quite ridiculous.”
Kim also warned Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast -- remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
Analysts said the launch would be viewed as a show of force in response to the South Korean government’s diplomatic efforts, effectively rejecting engagement.
“Seoul called for easing tensions, but Pyongyang answered by escalating them,” Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP.
“The message is that the North is pursuing... confrontation in response to goodwill,” he added.
South Korea’s defense minister said on Tuesday the military had “a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages” to respond to the DMZ incident, without providing further detail.
The South’s Unification Minister, Chung Dong-young, also proposed talks to address issues along the border to Pyongyang on Friday.
Kim Yo Jong, however, dismissed Chung’s suggestion of talks as a “wild dream and unilateral jargon.”
The flare-up comes at a sensitive time when US President Donald Trump’s recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that Seoul -- an ally of Washington -- could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North.
South Korea’s opposition People Power Party on Friday accused Lee of failing to criticize Pyongyang when warranted even as he takes a hard line on Ukraine for publicly disclosing the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war, an arrangement Seoul believed should be confidential.
“South Korean soldiers have been injured, and far from receiving an apology, we have been mocked by North Korea,” the opposition party said in a statement.
“We fail to see how selectively turning a blind eye to North Korea serves South Korea’s dignity or the safety of its people.”

item.description:
Dhaka, the densely populated capital of Bangladesh, ranked third among the world’s most polluted cities on Saturday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 170 at 9:14am.
The city’s air was classified as "unhealthy", indicating a health threat, according to the AQI report.
Pakistan’s Lahore, India’s Kolkata and Delhi occupied the first, second, and fourth spots on the list, with AQI scores of 214, 190, and 168 respectively.
According to the AQI scale, a reading between 50 and 100 is considered "moderate", with generally acceptable air quality, though sensitive individuals should limit prolonged outdoor exertion. AQI levels of 101–150 are "unhealthy for sensitive groups", 151–200 are " unhealthy", 201–300 are "very unhealthy", and readings above 301 are considered "hazardous", posing severe health risks.
The AQI, which reports daily air quality, informs residents how clean or polluted the air is and highlights potential health effects. In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five key pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution. Air quality usually deteriorates in winter and improves during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that air pollution causes about seven million deaths worldwide each year, primarily from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections.
